Those proposing this measure have coolly assumed that it is one of benevolence and Justice, whereas it is one of injustice and evil. The proposition is in substance that the Government shall donate lands in the west to those who will settle upon them and this is to extend not only to citizens of the United States but also to foreigners before naturalization. In other words, all the immense domain of the United States is to be, hereafter, given away, as rapidly as settlers can be induced to settle upon it.

So great a change in the policy of the Governments regarding the public lands, challenges examination and judgment.

Government lands have heretofore been put in market at one dollar and twenty five cents per acre, in convenient quantities, and upon any that remained unsold for some time the price has been reduced. The privilege of priority of right to purchase has also been secured to actual settlers over others.

The proceeds of land sales have gone into the treasury of the United States to the average amount of three millions of dollars yearly, constituting revenue to reimburse the Government for outlays in acquiring the lands, for the expenses of their survey and management, and for the cost of providing local governments pending their settlement.

It is manifest that it is not necessary to give away the lands in order to secure their settlement. The whole history of the Territories contradicts such pretence; nor can it be claimed as probable that settlement will stop in future unless such inducement as the one proposed be held out by the government. The utmost that can be alleged, is, that by this measure settlement may be accelerated to some extent. But dissatisfaction with the rate at which States have grown up in the west would be unreasonable indeed and therefore there appears no reason for attempting to stymie their growth by extraordinary measures.

Again; whatever loss the treasury sustains by withdrawing the proceeds of the land sales, would have to be made up by increased taxation upon the people of the country. It is proposed that all shall be taxed to buy lands of the Indians, to manage our land system, to provide governments for the Territories, to protect the frontiers from savages &c. and then that the lands to which these outlays relate shall be given away to settlers although they can reasonably be made to contribute to ease the Treasury. This is neither justice nor policy.

The public lands are also strong support to public credit, and to squander them is to weaken the government.

And yet this Homestead project, was one of the leading measures of the Republicans and endorsed in their platform in 1850. "Free Farms," "LANDS for the Landless," "Homes for the Homeless," these were the cries gotten up to delude the ignorant and win votes. The poor were to be made rich by Government gift: if they would only put the "free-farm party" in power.

It would be well if the fact were more thoroughly comprehended than it seems to be, that the government can have nothing to bestow which it does not obtain in some way upon trust, from the people. It follows, that it is no part of its business to make donations, and that it is an outrage upon the equal rights of all and essentially unjust, to appropriate the public property without an equivalent, to individuals or class.

It is likely that the enormous pressure upon the Treasury for war outlays, will prevent the passage of homestead bill at this time, even by Republican Congress. But the measure has been proposed, and it deserves to be kept in mind and steadily opposed as one of the unjustifiable and furious measures of the party in power. It constitutes one of the just objections to that party and is a good reason for withdrawing power from its hands at the earliest opportunity.

The Presidential Question.

The Democratic - Pottsville - Standard

Justice to say that the Board will re-elect all
the old teachers who may so desire. This
is complimentary to the teachers, and doing
the Board due justice.


THE RAIN AND ITS EFFECTS.


It was little singular and quite co-
incidental that the rains began to fall in
earnest on the anniversary of our first flood.
Of course our streets are, as usual, in
horrible plight, and precisely as should be
expected when every drop of rain stands
where it falls. We want surface drainage
as much as we need big levees. Mud
is now very handy at every crosswalk and
on many of the main thoroughfares. The
city looks little dirtier than usual in con-
sequence of the sediment left last winter.
But give us two or three inches of mud, all
the time in preference to two or three feet
of water. We do not wish to enter again
upon the hydraulic sports of last winter.
We are not amphibious, though we then
came near this double existing state.


LEGISLATIVE AND SENATORIAL.


Several members of the incoming Legis-
lature have bespoken accommodations at our
hotels and in the course of next week, they
will begin to show their benign faces, in-
creasing in number daily until the day of
the organization. The Senatorial fight, to
take place early in the session, begins to
make little ripple on the political surface.
John Conness and Senator Phelps are still
the leading candidates, and one or the other
of these aspirants will doubtless carry off the
prize to Washington.


LEVEES COMPLETED.


Our levees are all ready to be tested, and
there is no doubt but that it would be for
the interest of Sacramentans if they were
thoroughly tried this winter. Nothing could
do so much towards the perfect restoration
of confidence as the rise of the waters a foot
or two above the high-water mark of last
year, provided the levees can stand the press.
If they are perfect surety against another
inundation, then the quicker the fact is
demonstrated by a great flood in our rivers
at once.

MESSAGE OF THE PRESIDENT TO CONGRESS.


Annexed will be found the message of
the President transmitted to Congress, on
the 18th inst, in relation to the condemned
Indians.


The President was anxious not to act
with so much clemency as to encourage
another outbreak of the savages, nor with
degree of severity which should be real
cruelty, and therefore at first ordered only
the execution of such Indians as had been
proved guilty of violating females, but
only two of this class were found. He then
directed that out of the three hundred con-
demned men, such should be selected as
were proved to have participated in massacres
as distinguished from participation in
battles. These amounted to forty, and
included two of the first-class, but as
one of them had been strongly recon-
mended to mercy, he ordered that only
thirty-nine should suffer the death penalty.


The President does not make any sug-
gestion in regard to the disposition of the
260 out of the 800 condemned Indians
whom he may be said to have reprieved,
nor in regard to the remaining parts of the
Sioux tribe, who have incurred the ever
lasting hatred of the settlers of Minnesota,
and who will almost certainly be sacrificed
if permitted to remain in the State.


MESSAGE OF THE PRESIDENT.


To the Senate of the United States:


In compliance with your resolution of Dec.
5, 1862, requesting the President to furnish the
Senate with all the information in his posses
sion touching the late Indian barbarities in the
State of Minnesota, and also the evidence in
his possession upon which some of the princi-
pal actors and head men were tried and con-
demned to death. I have the honor to state
that on receipt of said resolution I transmitted
the same to the Secretary of the Interior ac-
companied by note, a copy of which is here
with inclosed, marked "A," and in response to
which I received through that Department


a copy of which is herewith inclosed marked
"B." (already published.) I further state
that on the eighth day of November
last I received a long telegraphic dispatch
from Major Gen. Pope, of St. Paul, Minnesota,
simply announcing the names of the persons
sentenced to be hanged. I immediately tele-
graphed to have transcripts of the records in all
the cases forwarded to me, which transcripts,
however, did not reach me until two or three
days before the present meeting of Congress.
Meantime, I received, through telegraphic dis
patches and otherwise, appeals in behalf of the
condemned, appeals for their execution and
expressions of opinion as to the proper policy
in regard to them, and the Indians generally in
that vicinity, none of which, as I understand,
falls within the scope of your inquiry. After
the arrival of the transcript of records but be-
fore I had sufficient opportunity to examine
them, I received a joint letter from one of the
Senators and both of the Representatives from
Minnesota, which contains some statements of
fact not found in the records of the trials, and
for which reason I transmit a copy marked
"C." (Already published.) I also for the
same reason inclose printed memorial of the
citizens of St. Paul, addressed to me, and for-
warded with the letter aforesaid. Anxious to
not act with so much clemency as to encourage
another outbreak on the one hand, nor with
so much severity as to be real cruelty on the
other, I caused a careful examination
of the records of the trials to be made, first
demanding the execution of such as had been proved
guilty of violating females. Contrary to my ex-
pectations, only two of this class were found.
I then directed further examination and clas-
sification of all who were proven to have partici
pated in massacres as distinguished from par-
ticipation in battles. This class numbered forty,
and included two convicted of female violation.
One of the number is strongly recommended by
the Commission which tried him for commu-
tion to ten years imprisonment. I have ordered
the other thirty-nine to be executed on Friday,
the 10th inst. The order was dispatched from
here on Monday, the 8th inst., by a messenger
to Gen. Sibley, and copy of which order is
herewith transmitted, marked "D." An abstract
of the evidence as to the forty is herewith in-
closed marked "E."


To avoid the immense amount of copying, I
lay before the Senate the original transcripts of
the records of the trials as received by me.
This is as full and complete response to the
resolution as it is in my power to make.


Signed ABRAHAM LINCOLN.

CAMP NEAR CHASECITY, Va. Nov. 1, 1862.—
ESfor Star: I send you a short account of the
little fight that occurred in our front, near
Aldie, on yesterday afternoon, in which the
1st Jersey took its usual share. The 1st
cavalry brigade, in two demi-brigades, one
consisting of the 1st Pennsylvania Cav'y, the
10th New York Cavalry and a section of Schir-
ler's Mounted Battery, under Colonel
Jones, of the 1st Pennsylvania; the other com-
posed of the 1st New Jersey Cavalry, the 90th
New York Harris Light Cavalry and another
section of artillery, under command of our
Lieutenant Colonel, the brave Joseph Karge, had
been sweeping the country from Aldie to Upper
Monocacy, driving in the enemy pickets and taxing
few prisoners. After doing this for two days,
on the 31st we were in bivouac a short distance
east of Aldie. Part of the 1st Rhode Island
Cavalry, belonging to General Stoughton's com-
mand, by some inconceivable carelessness,
allowed the enemy to surprise them. They were
their horses unsaddled and their arms laid aside; and
the first intelligence that we received of any
hostile force being in the neighborhood was
brought by fugitives rushing past us. In disorder
Karge immediately had his force under arms
and in five minutes the 1st Jersey were pushing
through the town, led by MAJOR Beaumont,
who were our pickets, under Captain X. S. Wren,
holding the enemy in check. Our fellows
charged fiercely upon the rebels and drove
them back upon their reserve, and driving the head
of the reserve back in confusion. Having thus
secured good position beyond the town, the
Jerseys formed at the foot of a hill, deployed
skirmishers regularly, and kept the rebels in
check. In the mean time, Colonel Karge brought
up the Harris Light and formed them as a
reserve. The enemy were visible along the
Snickersville road as far as the eye could reach,
and they had already deployed strong columns
on both sides of the road, in the woods and
fields. The rebels made vigorous effort to
drive us from our position, three several times
attempting to deploy in a cornfield to our left,
and three several times our skirmishers dashed
right into them, and drove them back in dis-
order, with loss. After holding the ground for
three quarters of an hour with cavalry alone,
under heavy fire of round shot, grape and
shrapnel we succeeded in bringing our section
into position, and inflicted further damage upon
the enemy, who were unable to do anything
with their strong force against the front shown
by our few men—the whole demi-brigade at
that time numbering only seven hundred and
fifty men. About an hour before sunset, Colonel
Karge received an order from Brigadier General
Bayard to fall back. The Colonel, however,
held the ground until nightfall, when the rebel
infantry, slowly pushing along the wooded hill
sides, were gradually flanking us. Our men
then withdrew in splendid order, a force of
carbineers remaining in the town until the
General sent them peremptory order to fall
back. The object of our reconnaissance having
been already accomplished, we returned to
camp that evening, having only eleven men
killed, wounded and missing. Captain SAWYER,
while leading the skirmishers with his usual
boldness, was painfully, but not dangerously
wounded. Sergeant Whitfield Lam, of Com-
pany H, was hit in the same manner. Orderly
SERGEANT Louis Fahs, of Company H, was killed.

Nitehen, though it was his first field, won high
credit by his goodness and intelligence, acting
aid to Lieut. Colonel Karge. Captains Lucas
and Keister managed their pickets admirably.
Lieuts. Maulsbury and Brooks, with their
skirmishers, faced superior numbers, and held
an exposed position for an hour, and until
recalled. Major Beaumont again won admi-
ration for his dash and judicious management of
the gallant men and officers entrusted to him;
Lieut. Karge was everywhere, doing everything, just
when and where he was needed. The Harris
Light did all they had to do with a steadiness
that was remarkable, when we remember the
number of raw recruits included in their force—
a renewed proof of the propriety of filing old
regiments rather than forming new; but
had it not been for the 1st Jersey, for the rapidity
with which it got ready for action, the dash
with which it went into action, and the stead-
iness with which it wheeled and formed after
the disorder of a charge up and down hill, the
whole command would have been taken at
great disadvantage, and probably been cut to
pieces by the mere weight and impetuosity of
the Confederate attack.

FROM THE 12TH REGIMENT.

WASHINGTON, Oct 10, 1862.
Dear Free Press,

The camp of the Twelfth, at Brattleboro, presented busy appearance last Tuesday morning. The thousand operations preparatory to breaking up of camp were in active progress. The quarters were full of friends of the soldiers, many of them ladies, who re seated here and there and plying busy fingers in taking the last stitches for their brothers and friends before bidding them the last good bye. The men were generally in good spirits and anxious to go. By eleven o'clock, every knapsack was packed and the regiment in line, and a half past eleven—the time set, to a minute—it marched from Camp Lincoln.

The day was a very hot one, and the sun blazed down, with midsummer power. The Thirteenth, Col. Randall, escorted the regiment to the depot. Col. Houghton, the acting Brigadier General of the post, took command of the column, and in order probably to show the regiment to some of his Brattleboro friends, took them by circuitous route through the streets to the depot. The march of nearly two miles in the hot sun was a pretty hard one for the boys but as they passed the depot, where I was stationed on special duty, I was glad to see that the company marched as stoutly as the stoutest, and that there in the little party were no stragglers. Perhaps twenty or thirty in all who had fallen out on the way, and who brought up the rear there was not one of the Howard Guard. Through some unseasonable neglect of the railroad companies, though the day and hour of our departure had been set for nearly a week, no cars were in readiness to take the regiment, and we had to wait until they were brought in below. The regiment was accordingly marched halt down the river to a shaded meadow, and allowed to lie off for the remainder of the day. A barrel of good things sent from Burlington by Mr. Beash, supplied our company with all they could eat, and to spare for the rest, and the afternoon passed comfortably away. At six o'clock, a train of empty cars arrived, and the work of embarkation commenced at seven. The cars were too few in number however. Some freight cars had to be rugged with seats manufactured on the spot, I believe our officers considered themselves fortunate not having to wait until cars and all were manufactured for the occasion, and it was ten o'clock before we were fairly under way. Before this, our kind friends had taken their leave by the trains in each direction, and the actual departure was as quiet as that of any train of thirty loaded cars.

Let me mention here the kind offices of your townsman, Wm. Brinsmaid, who took up his quarters with us on Monday, worked like beaver in helping the boys pack up their things, took charge of big pile of valises and bundles to be taken home, and remained till the last man in camp to pick up things and see that all was in proper shape. It was a valuable bit of service.

The delay in getting away was disgraceful on the part of the railroad managers; but was a fortunate thing for the regiment. Had it been packed away into the cars, as it came heated from the march, and been compelled to ride all the remainder of that hot day, the men would have suffered. As it was, they lay around in the shade during the afternoon, and the rail in the cool moonlight, and had the pleasure of a daylight boat-ride through the Sound. The night was a splendid one, and the ride down the beautiful valley of the Connecticut, which seemed doubly beautiful in the liquid moonlight, was a notable one for every man who had a particle of sentiment in his soul.

At Springfield (which we reached about 10 o'clock) we were received with rousing salute of 50 guns. Preparations had also been made on the supposition that we should arrive about supper-time, to supply refreshment to the troops; but the delay upset the kind arrangement. We made little stop there or anywhere, but swept on down the river. We reached New Haven at 2 o'clock, spent exactly an hour in changing the men and the baggage from the cars to the large and splendid steamer "Continental," and were off for New York. The boat barely touched at Peekskill, and then went on to Jersey City, where we debarked about noon. Col. Howe had provided us dinner of soup and bread, which was served promptly, and we were off again by rail for Washington.

I can give little time and space to the thousand times told story of the passage of the regiment from New York to Washington. We had the customary waving of handkerchiefs and hats, demonstrations of God-speed all along the way, the usual and—and it is all the more noticeable and praiseworthy because it is usual—substantial welcomes in the shape of hot coffee, good bread and butter, and meat, etc., served by the kind hands of the ladies and gentlemen of the Union Relief Association, in Philadelphia; and the customary delays in getting from Baltimore to Washington. Up to Baltimore we made steady and reasonably rapid progress, reaching there at six o'clock Thursday morning. Then came a march of a mile and a half across the city, six hours of tedious standing with stacked arms near the Washington depot, varied by breakfast at the Relief Rooms, when we were slowed away in freight cars and started out of the city. The train took 600 other troops besides our regiment, and numbered 81 heavily loaded cars, the men covering the tops as well as filling the insides of the cars. We made slow progress, waiting three or four hours at Annapolis Junction, and reached Washington at 10 o'clock Thursday night. Supper was given us in the not very sweet, or savory halls of the "Soldiers Rest" and in the huge whitewashed barns attached thereto, the boys finally laid themselves down to sleep as best they might, on the hard floors, many preferring to take their blankets and sleep on the ground outside. To-day we are to go into camp, somewhere about Washington, exactly where I cannot say at this present writing.

FrEAEcEs.-Under this head the Gin
cinnati Gazette of the 4th inst. has a
leader, in which some wholesome truths
are set forth in style as forcible as
truthful, and in which we most heartily
concur. The article is too long for our
columns to day. but we publish few
paragraphs upon one point, which is
and has been for some time agitating
the public mind. Intending to aid this
agitation until productive of change
for the better, is our reason for fur
nishing the following extracts in which
our readers will fnd more truth than
poetry:


The pay Of a private is S13 month,
and if we include his rations-which
are only sufficient for his subsistence
at the Communication price, thirty cents
each, his pay and subsistence amount
to S23 month; while the pay, rations
and servants allowance of. a Second
Lieutenant and Brevet Second-Lieuten :
ant of Infantry amount to Sl05 so a
month, of a First-Lieutenant to S110
so, and of a Captain to $3.50 so.


There is no justice in this wide dis
parity in the pay of men and officers.
Out of companies and regiments of in
experienced men, officers from Lieuten-
ant to Colonel of no more than the
average capacity--perhaps less-are
chosen, who Immediately are put on pay
from FIVE to ten times higher then the
rest. No one will pretend that there is
any reason for this disproportion. Its
effects upon the morals of the army is
bad. Its injustice is apparent and de-
pressing to the patriotism Of the men,
while it demoralizes the officers into
mercenaries who naturally come to have
more regard for the continuance Of their
salaries and rank than for the vigorous
prosecution and end of the war.


The pay of our commissioned officers
is such that to enlist as an officer is no
evidence Of patriotism. To enlist as
private soldier is evidence of patriotism.
Consequently the patriotism Of the
ranks is much higher than that of the
officers. This fact every one knows
who has observed our volunteer army.
As to the regular army, although there
are honorable exceptions, yet patriotic
sentiments are not regarded as in the
question at all. 1t is plain talking, and
it is unfortunate for the few honorable
exceptions in the regular army, and it
is not a pleasing reflection for the coun-
try, but the fact is patent that regular
army as purely mercenary in its nature
and feelings as any Swiss corps Of
palace guards, has resulted from our
military institutions and the political
Decentralization which has SO long con-
trolled them.


II there were no economical neces-
sites in the question, the reduction Of
the pay OF commissioned officers one
third or one-half would be necessary to
raise the morale Of the army, and any
apprehensions of evil consequences will
seem absurd on reflection. Will the
volunteer Colonel or Captain be likely
to resign because his inordinate pay is
reduced one-half, when his peer in every
respect is in the ranks, receiving only
Sl3 month? And if it should drive
out those who have entered the army for
the pay, and gil their places by promo
tious from the ranks. what an improve
ment will be made by this economical
measured The same will apply to the
regular officers. The country need
not desire any who are disposed to go
to stand on the order of their going.

leader, in which some wholesome truths
are set forth in style as forcible as
truthful, and in which we most heartily
concur. The article is too long for our
columns to-day, but we publish few
paragraphs upon one point, which is
and has been for some time agitating
the public mind. Intending to aid this
agitation until productive of change
for the better, is our reason for furnishing the following extracts in which
our readers will find more truth than
poetry:


The pay of a private is $13 a month,
and if we include his rations—which
are only sufficient for his subsistence
at the Communication price, thirty cents
each, his pay and subsistence amount
to $23 a month; while the pay, rations
and servants allowance of a Second
Lieutenant and Brevet Second-Lieutenant of Infantry amount to $105 so a
month, of a First-Lieutenant to $110
so, and of a Captain to $135 so.


There is no justice in this wide disparity in the pay of men and officers.
Out of companies and regiments of inexperienced men, officers from Lieutenant to Colonel of no more than the
average capacity—perhaps less—are
chosen, who immediately are put on pay
from FIVE to ten times higher than the
rest. No one will pretend that there is
any reason for this disproportion. Its
effects upon the morals of the army is
bad. Its injustice is apparent and depressing to the patriotism of the men,
while it demoralizes the officers into
mercenaries who naturally come to have
more regard for the continuance of their
salaries and rank than for the vigorous
prosecution and end of the war.


The pay of our commissioned officers
is such that to enlist as an officer is no
evidence of patriotism. To enlist as
private soldier is evidence of patriotism.
Consequently the patriotism of the
ranks is much higher than that of the
officers. This fact every one knows
who has observed our volunteer army.
As to the regular army, although there
are honorable exceptions, yet patriotic
sentiments are not regarded as in the
question at all. It is plain talking, and
it is unfortunate for the few honorable
exceptions in the regular army, and it
is not a pleasing reflection for the country, but the fact is patent that the regular
army is purely mercenary in its nature
and feelings as any Swiss corps of
palace guards, has resulted from our
military institutions and the political
decentralization which has so long controlled them.


If there were no economical necessities in the question, the reduction of the pay of commissioned officers one
third or one-half would be necessary to
raise the morale of the army, and any
apprehensions of evil consequences will
seem absurd on reflection. Will the
volunteer Colonel or Captain be likely
to resign because his inordinate pay is
reduced one-half, when his peer in every
respect is in the ranks, receiving only
$13 a month? And if it should drive
out those who have entered the army for
the pay, and fill their places by promotion from the ranks, what an improvement will be made by this economical
measure? The same will apply to the
regular officers. The country need
not desire any who are disposed to go
to stand on the order of their going.

He proceeded to the boarding house of the officer and there finding the woman, asked if she was ready to go home. The woman replied that she was, but that the federal officer in whose service she was would not permit her. The citizen then told the officer and received from him that the woman would be sent to him. This promise of the double dealing and bad faith of the officer, the citizen laid his complaint before Lieutenant Weitze, who manifested great indignation against the officer and requested the citizen to call Gen. Butler. The wife of our citizen undertook the mission to Gen. Butler and after difficulty succeeded in obtaining interview with him. Gen. Butler immediately took the matter in hand, and sent guard to the boarding house where the slave harbored, had the officer who harbored her jailed, and the interference of the chaplain of the federal regiments against the arrest of the woman had his credentials also arrested and placed in confinement. The girl sent home to her master with the request that she should not be cruelly punished. This the part of the General commanding calculated to put stop to an abuse which must produce quite as much trouble if it will be followed up in all similar cases of intermeddling with slaves.

Last week Colonel Shafer preferred charges against Robinson, lieutenant in the Fourteenth Maine regiment, who had been in charge of sick soldiers ordered North—to wit: among other things, that Robinson had told the sick men that there would be difficulty in procuring passage; but that they were willing to pay "something," and it was quite possible he could arrange matters to their entire satisfaction. Robinson, with another scoundrel, had succeeded in obtaining from Ave fifteen dollars from the soldiers, raising some two hundred dollars. Colonel Shafer laid these facts before General Butler, who sent for Robinson and compelled him to resign and remove his shoulder straps.

In the progress of the case, a man called Gen. Butler, and reported that a slave girl fifteen years old, was living with an officer of the United States army. The transaction is just such one as occurs in every state and every county of every State often in a month. If the pleas with which all similar "intermeddling with our slaves" should be allowed up, there would be excitement in this town. Don't you think so, neighbor? Intermeddling is not common practice, then sign and have nothing. We shall not follow this matter any further.


From the New Orleans Picayune, July 20

The information upon which we made the statements in the paragraph alluded to—given in our issue of Saturday morning, derived from an authority we could not question; and whatever of error there may be in it, is entirely unintentional on the part of the informant. We are happy to learn, as we do by the following letter, that the statement is circumstantially accurate. The following letter, by request of Major General Butler, corrects the statement.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE NEW ORLEANS PICAYUNE

HEADQUARTERS, DEPARTMENT OF THE GULF,
New Orleans, July 10, 1862.

As an editorial in your issue of this morning, titled "A warning TO intermediaries," contains several statements of facts, directed by the Major General commanding to make the following statement in regard to the case, with the request that you will give it publicity through your columns: The young slave girl indicated entered into the quarters of a United States officer in direct violation of general order prohibiting such conduct and evidently for improper purposes. An attempt afterwards made by another colored woman of questionable character to conceal the young girl. Subsequently the mistress called upon the General and, instead, you say, of her experiencing some difficulty in obtaining admittance to him, he sent to her carriage to her, considering her being ill. Upon leaving the particular of the case, he asked the girl if she was willing to go home to her mistress, well treated there; upon her expressing such readiness, he sent her in charge of an orderly to her old home. Your statement in relation to the arrest of the chaplain of the regiment is entirely incorrect; no such arrest was ever made. I have the honor to be, very respectfully, your obedient servant,

F. BUTLER, Commanding.

from the Cork Herald April 15.


Among the passengers who arrived at Queenstown
from New York, per the steamer Edinburgh, Wednes-
day evening (16th June), elderly and a
little boy of six years, she brought with her large
trunk bearing the inscription, Michael Roman Mouatrea
No II. On coming ashore she appeared in very weak
and uneasy state and was rumoured among the other
passengers that she had left her husband in New York,
or he perhaps was coming to her native place—supposed
to be a young recruit her shattered constitution.
Immediately after her arrival she engaged lodgings for
the night for herself and died at house in the Old
Square and after drinking a glass of porter went to bed.
Next morning apprehension of some unforeseen
evil was excited by the child coming from
his mother's room and complaining to the pro-
prietress of the lodgings that "Mamma would
not speak to him." She speedily thereupon proceeded
to her lodger's room, and found her lying in bed a
lifeless corpse. Medical aid was called in, but died.
The police were thereupon informed of the dis-
covery and they endeavoured by questioning the child to
elicit the real destination of the deceased. Owing
however to the little fellow's imperfect articulation he
could only to understood to say that his mother
was then doomed. It was expedient to examine the
contents of her trunk with a view to discovering
a clue to her identity. The only matter however, that
could be found likely to afford such clue was a letter
addressed to Daniel Bien Gonna, county Cork, Ireland,
but the police refrained from opening it for the present.
The other articles which the chest contained were chiefly
cheap dresses, numerous collection of portraits, several
presents for her at home, and some small house-
hold utensils. While the unfortunate child remains
in the lodgings and should the identity of the latter not
be discovered must be handed over to the relieving off-
icer for maintenance. On referring to the list of pass-
engers by the Edinburgh, the names which are thought to be
those of the deceased and her child are found to be Mrs
Hally or Hally and child.

saults the Davis Administration. The managers of that sheet know best whether they can afford, in their present predicament, to be hypercritical, and the preeminently factious of a faction; but as neither they, nor those to whom they appeal, have ever submitted, either in public or private affairs, to the semblance of control, it is not probable that considerations of Confederate safety will keep one pair of duelling pistols in their cases. The secession of these States was caused by a general passion for politics, which, in a slaveholding community, commonly is the only avenue to distinction, and to the intelligent the only solace of an intolerable, nightmare life in deathlessness. Secession, itself the offspring of politics, breeds in its turn a progeny of parties, each prolific of cliques, and each incapable of guidance. Mr. Davis has not warmed the stool of Office, before this aspirant or that newspaper seeks to push him from it; and score of men think themselves as well entitled to the elevation as he is. And their necks as precious as his? Why should he come in for the robes of office and they for rags?

Why he for incense and they for emptiness?
They made him, great as he is grown; their
votes are the meat upon which he has fed.

"Why," some scion of an ancient and dilapidated Virginia house might ask, "why is this man sovereign and I only sergeant upon promise of quarter pay?" It is in this key a kind of mad minor that The Wig pipes its dissatisfaction. "Why has my advice been followed?" asks the Able Editor of that paper. "Why does not the army ravage Pennsylvania?" And then it goes on frankly to declare why: it is because the Government, of course, isn't expected to even go through the motions of governing—has been "wrangling with popular Generals and bidding over petty jobs." This is acidulous as well as alliterative. The Wig then, really quite after the manner of Sir Philip (Junius) Francis, says; "a child with a bauble, an old man with a young wife, are partial illustrations of our deplorable folly." The rage for fine writing has led many a Southern editor into scrapes either droll or murderous; but this man of metaphor who has contrived to compare the Confederacy to "a bauble" and an "old man's wife" has surpassed all his predecessors as much in boldness as in truth.

To say that The Wig is discontented, exasperated, indignant, and ferocious is to say nothing adequate. Its wrath mounts to ecstasy. Summer and Winter have been passed in dreary inaction. Disillusion and weariness have demoralized the Confederate camps. The "finest army ever assembled" has wasted away. Still The Richmond Wig has borne it with a patient shrug. But now, Patience being no longer Virtue, but the most vicious of Vices, The Wig takes off its coat and delivers its right and left at the culpable CABINET assuring it, readers, that certain "reputable great men" are, after all, disreputable little men, who must, unless this fine, fresh, youthful Confederacy is to go to the deuce, be reformed out of Office, and give place to those who read The Richmond Wig regularly and profit by its admonitions. It calls upon Congress to see that other departments perform their "functions" and confidently predicts that when "our side" gets inside, the vehicle will move with admirable ease and celebrity. But if "Congress" should prove quite as incompetent as "Cabinet," nothing will remain to be done but for Jefferson Davis to go up to the House, pistol the Speaker, turn out the Members, and establish Despotism tempered by cocktails and leading articles.

This is the Confederacy, so little compact that even the perils of war and imminent destruction cannot unite it. These are the men so little unselfish, so grossly selfseeking, that their own companions cry shame upon their low ends and little aims. These are the proofs of capacity for maintaining political independence which the Rebels offer to the powers of the world—President, Cabinet, Senators, Representatives, Editors, squabbling like a group of runaway boys, over a birds nest with nothing in it. Why, this would make the most brilliant victories barren—what will be its effect, when thick coming defeats, the occupation of great cities, the dispersion of the Rebel armies, the seizure of the military strongholds, the complete command of coasts and rivers and gulfs, shall have brought that bitter disappointment to which only despair can succeed? Let the Rebel leaders look well to themselves then, for the popular petard which they have been examining with falsehoods and passions, may then give them a hoist more lofty than palatable.

HOSPITALS AT RICHMOND.—The Fayetteville Observer, says:

We have reason to know that many of the hospitals here are very loosely conducted that the wants of many of the wounded are badly attended to—that some, if not many, of the wounded are sorely neglected. The want of cleanliness in the hospitals and among them, if continued during the remaining months, may produce pestilence.

In consequence of these abuses appear to be an insufficient number of Surgeons and nurses; the fact that too many of the Surgeons have been appointed because of something else than merit; the criminal neglect of some of them to make the best of all the talent, skill, and man-power at their disposal, however small that may be; in very many instances an improper consumption of, in part, some Surgeons and nurses of medicines intended for the patients.

We allude to this in the hope that the Government may, in its discretion to this department, see that medical affairs in Richmond be not worse managed than any other.

We have heard these charges alleged before, and are convinced that there is some ground for them. At all events there should be rigid investigation. The Surgeon General should appoint an Inspector of Hospitals or other officer charged with the special duty of visiting the various hospitals as often as practicable and reporting upon their condition, management, etc. He should be a conscientious, industrious man who would discharge this duty "without fear, favor or prejudice." He should request all persons who have charge to prefer any complaints made to him in order that they may be investigated. He should ascertain which of the surgeons, if any, are responsible for any rigors of the wounded men. He should inquire into the disposition of the deceased and prescribe such regulations as would prevent the improper consumption of medicines intended for patients, etc.

We have not the slightest expectation, possible, that our suggestion will be heeded by the powers; thus, we beg the contrary. We believe that things will be permitted to go on so long as they are, until a cloud of grief, in the shape of repeated complaints, is heaped upon the back of the Surgeon General. He will then be soon to move, when, perhaps, it may be needless to go so far.

Admitting the right of blockade as a temporary war measure, every government of Europe has addressed itself to promote the free navigation of rivers and entrance to ports. The officers and members of El Dorado County Agricultural Society have much to be proud of. We congratulate them on the success which has crowned their efforts. The number, variety, size and beauty of the articles exhibited at their Fourth Annual Fair cannot be excelled in any county in the State. The tables were loaded with the products of vineyard, orchard and garden. It is admitted that the fruits and wines of El Dorado, in favor and quality, cannot be excelled. This fact was admitted by visitors from distance, many of whom were present. In the exhibit of stock and stock only, did the Fair fall short of expectation; in all other respects it far exceeded it. We have shown what can be done with limited means and no State aid—extent to the Society the latter, and it would not fall much behind the State Fair. A new interest has been awakened; success has largely increased the number of members, and hereafter the Society will be able, without the fear of embarrassment, offering more and larger premiums which will of course, increase the number of exhibitors.

The stock parade on Wednesday and Thursday; carriage horses in harness and saddle horse; not very large yet it was witnessed with unusual interest. Enemies of the society predicted failure, and thus prevented timid persons from entering stock until too late. After the entries had been closed, we are informed the Secretary was solicited to allow new entries, which he could not do, according to the rules of the Society, however much he desired fine display of stock. The parade was headed by the Band, and marshaled by Messrs. Henry, Fountain, Webster, Hornblower, Condee and Brewster. It started from the stock grounds on Sacramento street, and passed through Main street, in front of the Pavilion, to Upper Placerville and back.

On Thursday afternoon, at 3 o'Clock, a large crowd of ladies and gentlemen assembled at the race course, to witness the equestrian skill of the lady competitors for the different prizes. The competitors were Miss Hornblower, Miss Cary, Mrs. Fountain, and Mrs. Hooker. Much interest was manifested in the result, and from the eager and animated appearance of the spectators, it was plainly perceptible that they anticipated an exciting contest, in which they were not disappointed. Each lady rode gracefully, and fearlessly and handled the reins skillfully. This was one of the most pleasing features of the Fair, attracted most interest and gave most satisfaction. Each side of the track was lined with carriages and buggies, filled with ladies. Good order was preserved and no coarse expression used. The prizes we believe were judiciously awarded—at least such is the judgment of the spectators.

We regret to state that Miss Hornblower was thrown from her horse. While riding along rapidly, a dog rushed across the track and struck her horse, causing him to shy and stumble and unseat his rider. She was not seriously injured, we are glad to learn.

The horse racing did not amount to much, the sum being too inconsiderable to make it worth contending for. But little interest was manifested in the first race, it being taken for granted that the horse the "boys" were backing would take the prize, which he did by scratch, notwithstanding the determined efforts of the rider of the beaten horse to hold him back. Had the rider broken the beaten horse would have distanced the winning nag. We left the ground with the impression that it is dangerous sometimes to bet on a "dead thing."

During the past week we have had calls from Lauman, of the Lansing Argus, Merrill of the Prairie du Chen Courier, and Cover of the Grant County Herald. These gentlemen all had the appearance of representing good CONSTITUENCIES, and seemed as light-hearted and happy as any other man. Lauman has been out on the frontier, at the junction of the Milwaukee and the Menominee, where there is said to be smart trading post, rejoicing in the ambitious name of Cream City. We are indebted to Robert Grant, of this city for brief abstract of the acts of the Clayton County board of Supervisors. Board was in session four weeks; it was working session. About 400 diff. erent claims against County and other matters presented to them were disposed of. $4,000 was appropriated for building County Jail; $4,000 for fire proof Treasurer and Recorders Office; $4,000 for District Court Room at Elkader. These appropriations being the extent to which the board is limited by law, they were made contingent upon the citizens of Elkader and the county at large contributing liberally in money and sites for the buildings in private way. The amount of personal property assessments in the county for this year foots up $188,192.15, being some $50,900 more than last year. The country back of US, one week ago Thursday night had severe drenching, the lightning cut up terrific tantrums in the air, the rain fell in torrents, and little babbling brooks became for few moments, mad torrents. An extra from the Star of the West Office, New Oregon, brings us the intelligence that the Turkey river in less than eight hours rose over twenty feet, and the rushing waters carried away the fine bridge across the stream at that point, which cost $4,000. Munson & Pearce lost large quantity of lumber, their mill was saved in somewhat damaged condition. The Decorah Republic reports several cows killed by the electric fluid, the barn of Mr. Jennish, who lives near Decorah was also shattered by one of these quick falling bolts. Up on Frankville Prairie where water is seldom seen, the flood cut up queer antics, carrying away miles of rail fences. The same facts existed on Washington Prairie. The Sheriff had warded off a good many blows from him, and now urged him to fly for his life. Some one else cried out "Run! Run!" At this he started towards the post Office, and on his way a shower of stones was hurled after him, one of them striking him on the side of the head, just above the temple. This partially knocked him down, but he scrambled up again, and soon he was struck on the back of the head with another stone, but he soon reached the post Office, and was admitted inside, after which the shutters were closed, and Mr. Pors was sent down cellar.

The mob meantime came up and demanded admittance, but the post office clerk would not open the doors, and told them upon his honor, that Mr. Pors was not inside. The mob were fairly raving about this time and began to talk about threats, and actually supposed his last hour had come. In his own language, as he told it to us, "I tell you," says he, "I said my last prayer in that cellar, knowing, as I do, the ferocity and brutality of a mob."

Soon the mob returned to the Court House, and began to tear up the enrollment lists. While they had thus been diverted, Mr. Pors was carried off in a buggy, there being only one man in the place who was willing to take the responsibility of driving through the streets with Mr. Pors. The two took by way direction, and came right down the lake shore to this city. Before they had got far however, the buggy broke down, and they had to stop to repair it, Mr. Pors being meanwhile entirely exhausted from the wounds he had received, a good deal of blood having flowed from them.

The mob now came back to the post office, and were admitted, when they looked all through the building, and after seeing for themselves that Mr. Pors was gone, they went to the grist mill of Mr. Tomlinson, an American, whom the rioters charged with being an Abolitionist. He is a most worthy citizen, however, and had a fine mill, which cost him several thousand dollars. This they damaged to a great extent, and stole more or less money out of it. A German had warned him that the mob would kill him, and so he concealed himself in the mill, and finally got away from it in such a manner as to escape from the place. Mr. B. G. Hoyt, an American Republican, and a Free Mason, was also at the mill with Mr. Tomlinson, and he concealed himself behind a warehouse, where he remained some time, and finally he also escaped from the place, and came to this city yesterday. Mr. Vail, banker, an American Republican, and Free Mason, who had also been threatened, came here with Mr. Hoyt, bringing all the bank specie in a basket with him, and in his pockets.

After the mob left the mill they started towards Mr. Pors' residence, and on the way stopped at the residence of B. G. Hoyt, and began to boot and halloo.
